A cutting-edge instrument has been developed to model neuromorphic architectures and their underlying memristive devices at the circuit and device levels. This instrument, called NARS (Neuromorphic Architecture and memristive Routines Simulator), enables users to design and test various neural network topologies, including feed-forward, recurrent, and convolutional networks, and their memristive devices, such as CMOS-based memristors and spintronic devices. NARS's spin-off tool, MRS (Memristive Routines Simulator), facilitates the simulation of memristor devices in isolation. This instrument is particularly useful for researchers and engineers working on neuromorphic architectures and memristive devices. In this study, we introduce NARS and MRS, and provide a detailed explanation of their operation, along with an example application of NARS in simulating a memristive feed-forward neural network. Furthermore, we showcase the potential of NARS in analyzing and optimizing memristive neural networks. This work is significant for advancing the development of neuromorphic architectures and memristive devices. NARS and MRS are open-source software packages available for download at https://github.com/neuromorphic-ai/nars. We present initial findings from our examination of Haro 14, a starburst galaxy in the Local Universe, observed using the MUSE instrument. This study marks the first time a compact galaxy has been thoroughly investigated using integral field spectroscopy. Our results reveal that the galaxy's starburst core is primarily composed of young, hot stars with minimal dust content. However, the surrounding area is dominated by older stars with cold properties, suggesting the presence of a complex stellar population. This may indicate that the galaxy's starburst is not a unified whole, or that the galaxy has undergone a two-stage star formation process. Our analysis also shows that the galaxy's starburst is accompanied by a compact HII region surrounded by a diffuse halo of ionized gas extending up to 300 pc. This ionized gas is likely the result of a recent merger between the galaxy's starburst and its cold interstellar medium. This study's findings are consistent with the galaxy's recent merger history and its star formation processes. Further research using MUSE will allow for a more in-depth analysis of Haro 14's star formation processes and its surrounding environment. The dataset and code are freely available for public use. To better understand the creative potential of humans and machines, comprehensive research into creative cognition is necessary. Despite this, creative behavior remains poorly understood, particularly in areas where people use imaginative combinations of ideas to understand each other and interpret the world around them. To address this, we've developed a dataset called MetaCLUE, which contains over 20,000 examples of visual metaphors - a unique form of creative expression where people combine images to convey complex ideas. By using a combination of human judgment and computer algorithms, we've identified a set of 1,200 metaphors that can help us explore the underlying processes of imagination and creativity. Our study shows that creating these metaphors requires a range of cognitive and computational abilities, and we demonstrate how different approaches to machine learning can be used to analyze and generate them. The dataset and code for MetaCLUE are freely available for researchers to use. By examining visual metaphors and the processes that create them, we hope to gain a deeper understanding of the imagination and creativity. Our ultimate goal is to develop a tool that can help people generate new, original ideas. The widespread adoption of botnets has made them a significant threat to global digital security. As a result, researchers are focusing on developing more effective methods for identifying and detecting these networks. This study proposes a new approach to identifying botnets by analyzing honeypot command logs. By leveraging natural language processing techniques, our model can group IP addresses and determine whether they are likely to be part of the same botnet. Our experimental results show that our model's accuracy is comparable to existing state-of-the-art methods, despite the limited availability of relevant data. In addition, our analysis of command diversity and IP address clustering provides valuable insights into botnet behavior, even in the absence of clear results. This study demonstrates the potential of natural language processing techniques in botnet research, and we plan to further explore their application in future studies. The code and data used in this research will be made publicly available for others to use and build upon. The EarthNets initiative is designed to harness the capabilities of Artificial Intelligence in observing our planet, leveraging core Infrastructure as a Service principles and adhering to a Software as a Service paradigm to simplify access. EarthNets comprises a series of interconnected web services, each responsible for a specific observational aspect, such as providing satellite imagery or atmospheric data. These services are linked through a central Portal service, serving as the entry point for users, particularly researchers, to easily navigate and incorporate EarthNets services within their workflows. Developed using cloud-hosted technologies, EarthNets is built with a modular architecture that facilitates the addition of new services, ensuring a seamless integration process. In this paper, we introduce the EarthNets framework, outlining its underlying design, user interface, and implementation details, with a focus on demonstrating its potential utility through a case study involving remote sensing applications for COVID-19 research. Minimax offline RL is a promising direction, but faces significant challenges
when dealing with limited sample sizes. To address this issue, we introduce
the Limited Sample Examination (LSE) framework, which enables us to analyze
the thoroughness, rapid learning rates and first-order optimization capabilities
of offline RL algorithms under limited sample conditions. Our key findings
include: 1) LSE-based algorithms can still achieve optimal performance even
with an exponentially increasing number of samples, but only if the number
of model trajectory pairs is sufficiently large. 2) To overcome the challenges
associated with limited samples, we propose the Limited Sample Examination
Projection (LSE-Prox) algorithm, which can still achieve optimal performance
even with a polynomial number of samples. However, its effectiveness relies
on the size of the model trajectory pair set, which must be sufficiently
large. 3) To overcome the challenges associated with limited samples,
we propose the Limited Sample Examination Projection Gradient (LSE-ProxGD)
algorithm, which can achieve optimal performance even with a polynomial
number of samples. However, its effectiveness relies on the size of the
model trajectory pair set, which must be sufficiently large. Our theoretical
analysis provides a clear understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of offline
RL algorithms under limited sample conditions, and our experimental results
demonstrate the effectiveness of LSE-based algorithms in real-world scenarios.

A widely used statistical model for count, rate, and binary data is the tree-structured Poisson log-linear model, which is particularly effective in modeling rate variations within and between subjects. The model's flexibility, however, also makes it prone to overfitting, especially when working with large datasets. In this research, a new approach is presented to enhance model interpretability and prevent overfitting by considering the independence of model components and utilizing a tree-structured penalty term within a penalized likelihood framework. The proposed method is demonstrated to work effectively in both linear and generalized linear settings, and various penalty parameter estimation methods are discussed. The performance of the approach is evaluated using a real-world example of influenza incidence data, and simulations are conducted to compare the results with existing methods. The findings suggest that the proposed approach offers a reliable and computationally efficient solution for large-scale modeling applications. Temporal modeling in videos is a challenging task due to the vast number of frames that need to be processed.
Recent advancements in video understanding rely heavily on the application of Transformer architectures, but they often suffer from high computational costs and inefficient memory usage. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel approach called Gradient Forward-Transmission (GF-T). This method enables the simultaneous processing of large groups of videos within a single batch, resulting in significant improvements in both speed and memory efficiency. To achieve this, we develop a specialized forward-propagation technique that leverages gradient information to enhance model efficiency. Additionally, we design a scalable loss function to accurately capture temporal dependencies across large batches. Our proposed method can be applied seamlessly to various video understanding tasks, including action recognition and video retrieval. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of GF-T, showcasing substantial improvements in both accuracy and efficiency. The Semantic Web community has widely adopted SPARQL for querying the Web, but its current version falls short in meeting the demands of the growing number of applications that require more advanced features. These applications, such as the RDF Scene Graph, need a robust query language that can handle complex tasks like visual understanding and natural language processing. To address this limitation, we propose an extension to SPARQL, dubbed VGStore, which enhances its capabilities to support multimodal applications. Recent breakthroughs in adversarial training have significantly improved the resilience of models against subtle attacks. However, most methods are ineffective against sophisticated and tailored attacks that target vulnerabilities in specific areas of the model's map. This study presents a novel adversarial training approach, dubbed Latent Frontier (Ladder), which enhances the model's robustness to sophisticated and easier-to-eradicate attacks. Ladder achieves this by leveraging a modified version of the model's map, derived from the model's decision boundary, to identify and prioritize the model's most vulnerable areas. Furthermore, we propose a training objective that forces the model to recognize and differentiate between different levels of attack severity, thereby increasing its ability to detect and respond to both simple and complex attacks. Thorough experiments across multiple datasets have demonstrated that Ladder surpasses existing methods in improving both the model's ability to detect and resist both simple and sophisticated attacks. Additionally, we provide theoretical evidence to support the effectiveness of Ladder in mitigating the impact of both straightforward and sophisticated attacks. Cardiac disease caused by abnormal left ventricular function can be diagnosed with the help of echocardiogram imaging, which is a non-invasive method that provides valuable insights into the heart's left ventricle. However, the technical limitations of this method, such as low image quality and varying acoustic conditions, can make it difficult to obtain accurate measurements. To overcome this challenge, we propose a new deep learning-based approach that leverages a steerable pyramid transform to extract relevant features from echocardiogram images. Our proposed method first utilizes a steerable pyramid transform to break down the echocardiogram image into smaller, rotationally invariant components, known as pyramids. These pyramids are then used as the input to a tailored convolutional neural network to predict the key parameters of left ventricular function, such as volume, ejection fraction, and end-systolic and end-diastolic volumes. Our experimental results show that our proposed method outperforms the existing state-of-the-art approaches in terms of its ability to accurately measure left ventricular function parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method can effectively extract the key information from echocardiogram images using the steerable pyramid transform, even when the images are noisy and of poor quality. Our approach can be easily adapted for use with other medical imaging modalities, such as X-rays and magnetic resonance imaging. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to utilize the steerable pyramid transform to extract the key information from echocardiogram images and use it to develop a deep learning-based measurement system. Our study contributes to the field of medical image analysis and opens up new avenues for exploring the use of steerable pyramid transform in medical image processing and analysis. The task of categorizing avian species poses a significant challenge due to the vast diversity of bird species, which number over $10,000$ varieties. Furthermore, visual characteristics of birds can be highly similar, leading to low inter-class variability, which complicates classification. To address this issue, we developed a novel multistage classification pipeline that leverages transfer learning to efficiently categorize bird species. Our approach involves a two-stage classification process: the first stage employs a convolutional neural network to filter images into categories based on their beak shapes, which are then used to filter images into categories based on their plumage patterns in the second stage. Our multistage method demonstrates a notable improvement in accuracy, specifically a 2.5% increase in the AUC score, over a single-stage approach. Our multistage approach also exhibits a significant reduction in the number of required training examples, specifically a fourfold decrease, which is particularly beneficial for working with small datasets. Our multistage pipeline's efficacy is further validated by its successful application to the iNaturalist 2018 dataset, where it yields an accuracy of $85.7\%$ in the top-1 category and $83.2\%$ in the top-5 categories. This phenomenon has been proven to be exploitable in various studies. To address this problem, we have developed an innovative method called CacheQL that enables the detection of cache side channels in software. This method involves creating a specialized database to track the cache side channels in a given program. This tool allows for both the identification of potential vulnerabilities in software and the precise location of the specific lines that are vulnerable to such attacks. This technology has been successfully tested on a range of real-world applications, including a specific analysis of the Python programming language. This analysis revealed that the Python standard library is susceptible to cache side channels in software, which led to the identification of multiple vulnerabilities in widely used libraries. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of our method in quickly identifying cache side channel vulnerabilities in software, even in complex production software, and provides a clear path for further improvement in this area. This study explores the convergence of variational p-harmonic functions outside finite point sets towards p-harmonic functions, considering both the case where points are isolated and where there are a finite number of them, with corresponding convergence of Green functions in such instances. Our proof draws on a 2015 paper by Cherkaoui and Manfredi, yet our approach differs from that of the original authors, instead building on a 2019 paper by Castorina, Manfredi, and Zhang that identified a significant scale in p-harmonic functions. By leveraging this scale, we have developed a new, simplified proof of the original result. Moreover, this scale enables us to establish a new, critical finding that any measure with finite mass at a point will drive a variational p-harmonic function towards a p-harmonic function, except at that point. This new result can be seen as a form of the "strong King random phase" phenomenon, with implications for the existence of multiple p-harmonic functions on the same domain. Finally, we have also demonstrated that the original result fails for p=2.

We investigate the crosswise momentum weighted Sivers asymmetries in charged pion production from a polarized transversely polarized proton and a longitudinally polarized transversely polarized kaon within the context of a simplified model that accounts for spin-orbit correlations. A stealthy backdoor attack is launched against deep learning models by secretly embedding malicious triggers in the input, allowing the compromise of various classification models. Existing attacks either rely on fixed backdoor patterns or insert a predetermined pattern into the input. Our research presents DeepPayload, a novel, general-purpose backdoor attack that integrates any pre-trained deep learning model into a targeted model. This adaptable attack identifies the optimal shape and location of the embedded trigger within the target model, making it more difficult to defend against. Experimentally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of DeepPayload against multiple classification models, including image recognition and language models, achieving a success rate of up to 100% with small trigger sizes. Furthermore, our attack outperforms existing methods by up to 30% on CIFAR-10 and MNIST datasets. The source code for DeepPayload is publicly available on GitHub. Under specific circumstances, we also introduce a defensive technique called DeepPayload Defense that can detect backdoor attacks with a high level of accuracy. This detection method surpasses existing methods by up to 10% on MNIST. The corresponding defensive code for DeepPayload is available on GitHub. This model is based on a system of ordinary differential equations that describe the behavior of chromatin-bound proteins and the production of specific messenger RNA molecules. By applying this model to time course data from chromatin immunoprecipitation experiments, researchers can infer the behavior of these proteins. Specifically, a method is developed to estimate the rates at which specific RNA polymerase II proteins are recruited to promoters and the rates of mRNA transcription. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated using a large dataset of ChIP-experiment time course data. The results show that the proposed method is capable of accurately reconstructing the underlying processes that govern gene regulation. Additionally, a case study involving the human MHC class I gene reveals that the binding of TBP is highly stable, whereas the transcription of the gene itself is less consistent, indicating that gene expression is primarily driven by TBP recruitment, not its stability. The developed method is expected to facilitate a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between chromatin structure, protein binding, and gene regulation. This understanding can be used to design therapeutic strategies for diseases caused by aberrant gene expression. Furthermore, the model and the new method can be applied to other biological processes, such as gene promoter regulation. Recent advancements in tensor decompositions have led to the development of sparse tensor codes, such as Tensor-Flatten and Tensor-Compressed Matrices, offering improved compression and performance over traditional matrix-based schemes. Building upon these advancements, we introduce a new compression method called Dependency Driven Trace Examination (DDTE) that leverages the benefits of tensor decompositions and extends the functionality of existing codes. By incorporating DDTE into Tensor-Flatten and Tensor-Compressed Matrices, we achieve significant improvements in compression efficiency and vectorization capabilities. Notably, our results show that the modified Tensor-Flatten code reduces storage requirements by 70.6% and 46.7% compared to the original and Tensor-Compressed Matrices, respectively. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the DDTE-based Tensor-Flatten code achieves a 3.8x speedup in CPU-based GPU offloading, and a 2.9x speedup in mobile applications. These findings confirm the efficacy of DDTE in enhancing the compression and vectorization capabilities of tensor codes, opening up new avenues for future research and development. We introduce a novel spectral method for solving the fractional Schrödinger equation on an infinite domain. Utilizing the Grünwald-Letnikov approximation, this method transforms the fractional space derivative into a set of ordinary differential equations with high-order derivatives that are coupled. We derive explicit formulas for the method's coefficients and demonstrate its accuracy through numerical experiments on the infinite domain. Furthermore, we analyze the method's convergence properties and prove its stability in the context of the fractional energy space. Supporting numerical results validate our theoretical findings. This method is particularly well-suited for solving the quantum graph model, where the potential can be both bounded and unbounded. We showcase its effectiveness by solving a model of graphene with a delta potential and compare the results to those obtained using finite difference methods. Our results show that the spectral method is more accurate and efficient, particularly when using a small time step. We also apply the method to a model of graphene with an infinite potential well, observing excellent agreement with analytical solutions. Overall, this research demonstrates the spectral method's accuracy and efficiency on the infinite domain and highlights its advantages over finite difference methods. Additionally, the method's stability properties make it a suitable choice for solving the fractional Schrödinger equation on a bounded domain. In this research, we propose and investigate the use of trainable variants of Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs), called Trainable MFCCs (T-MFCCs), for speaker authentication tasks. T-MFCCs are created by applying neural networks to Mel spectrogram features. We examine the impact of varying network architecture, loss function, and optimisation criteria on speaker authentication performance. We compare speaker verification and verification with speaker-provided verification keys in a controlled experiment using the VoxCeleb dataset. Our results demonstrate that the proposed T-MFCCs can enhance speaker authentication and verification efficiency, yielding significant gains over traditional MFCCs, particularly in speaker verification tasks. Specifically, we achieve a 9.8% relative improvement in the Equal Error Rate (EER) and a 7.7% improvement in the Minimally Suppressive Detection Error Rate (mDER) on the VoxCeleb dataset. Our study also reveals that the loss function and network architecture have a substantial effect on the performance of T-MFCCs. Moreover, we observe that the proposed T-MFCCs can be learned from a single dataset without requiring pre-trained MFCCs, offering a more efficient and efficient solution. However, we also note that the proposed T-MFCCs can be more computationally expensive than traditional MFCCs. Our research contributes to the development of a new class of features for speaker authentication and speech processing, offering a more efficient and efficient solution. Graph neural networks can be broadly categorized into two types: those that utilize fixed graphs, such as those based on convolutional neural networks, and those that dynamically generate or modify graphs during inference, such as those based on graph attention networks. This framework enables efficient and effective modeling of complex dependencies in images, as well as the integration of external data for improved performance. Experimental results demonstrate the potential of this framework to achieve state-of-the-art performance on image segmentation tasks. The proposed method can also be applied to other models, such as Markov fields, as an efficient inference approach. Furthermore, the framework's modularity allows for the integration of other models, such as energy-based models, to facilitate a wide range of applications. A critical challenge in melanoma classification lies in the scarcity of large, annotated datasets, hindering the development of reliable computer-assisted diagnostic systems. To address this issue, we've created a distributed education platform that enables medical students to learn about melanoma classification while contributing to the annotation of melanoma skin lesion images. This platform, powered by the PHTrain protocol, allows students to learn through hands-on annotation tasks, with their contributions verified and potentially submitted to the ISIC dataset for research purposes. As students gain proficiency, their annotations are reviewed and utilized to refine their performance, providing them with a sense of accomplishment and progress. Through this initiative, we've collected 14,119 annotations from 1,136 individuals, 1,000 of which have been validated and incorporated into the ISIC dataset. By leveraging this educational pipeline, we're aiming to create a robust and diverse dataset for research, while providing medical students with a valuable learning experience. Furthermore, our approach enables students to contribute to the advancement of melanoma classification, ultimately supporting the development of more accurate diagnostic systems. By replicating this model, we believe that even smaller institutions can make a significant impact in this field. To facilitate replication, we're providing access to our annotation tools, guidelines, and recommendations for success. In the long term, we envision establishing a network of institutions collaborating to produce high-quality annotations for research purposes, while fostering a community-driven approach to melanoma classification. By pooling our resources, we can accelerate the creation of more accurate diagnostic systems, ultimately benefiting patients in their daily lives. To achieve this vision, we're committed to establishing a network of institutions, with a primary focus on developing educational materials and annotations for melanoma classification. We welcome collaborations from institutions, educational organizations, and professionals to join our initiative and drive forward this mission. An evaluation of these models has shown that state-of-the-art models outperform their traditional counterparts, achieving significant improvements in accuracy, particularly in tasks that involve modeling complex relationships between words, such as similarity and analogy. The SART benchmark is now available online, along with the code and pre-trained models, with the aim of advancing the field of word embeddings and encouraging further research and development. 3D point cloud data is widely used in various applications, but its efficiency and accuracy can be compromised due to limited storage and processing capabilities. This research introduces a groundbreaking, non-orthogonal multiple access technique for downlink transmissions, leveraging deep learning to optimize interference mitigation across multiple users. By employing a recurrent neural network to analyze channel state information, the scheme estimates residual interference at each user, then utilizes an fully connected network to predict the necessary mitigation, which is subsequently applied through successive interference cancellation. Results from extensive simulations demonstrate the proposed scheme's superiority over conventional approaches, such as zero-forcing and random interference cancellation. In particular, the study shows that the proposed scheme approaches the performance of an optimal baseline that maximizes signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio in an adaptive manner, while also being more computationally efficient. Overall, the findings indicate that non-orthogonal multiple access can achieve comparable performance to traditional methods with less complexity. Furthermore, the research explores the potential of adapting the mitigation factors to specific channel structures, which can lead to additional performance improvements. A dead pixel within an image sensor results in an incomplete measurement, leading to image degradation. Current methods for detecting dead pixels rely on comprehensive image scans using large receptive fields, which can be computationally demanding. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach that employs a single neural network to efficiently locate dead pixels with a receptive field focused on local areas. This approach enables the simultaneous identification of multiple dead pixels, even those situated near each other, without increasing computational complexity. Our method achieves this through the use of a small kernel size of 1x1, which we mitigate by introducing a feature aggregation module that extracts local features from multi-scale images. This module is designed to capture both fine and coarse image details, enabling our model to effectively detect dead pixels. Our method achieves superior results on the Dead Pixel Dataset and demonstrates comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods, while boasting a significantly reduced computational complexity. Additionally, we present an in-depth analysis of our method's performance and provide a detailed examination of its accuracy and speed. This work marks the first instance of using a single neural network to identify dead pixels with a localized receptive field. Our method is now available on the GitHub platform. To overcome the limitations of edge devices in processing deep neural networks (DNNs), a highly-efficient architecture called AppealNet has been developed. AppealNet optimizes the performance of DNN-based computer vision applications by leveraging the capabilities of edge and cloud resources. It achieves this through a novel approach that involves selectively transferring computations to the cloud while minimizing latency. AppealNet generates a dynamic selection map that identifies the optimal sections of a convolutional layer to outsource to the cloud, thereby reducing transfer latency. Additionally, AppealNet introduces a highly-efficient selection kernel that enables rapid, on-device transfer of partial feature maps to the cloud, resulting in significant improvements in latency and energy efficiency compared to existing approaches. Experimental results demonstrate that AppealNet achieves a remarkable 2.5 to 4.5 times reduction in latency and a 2.5 to 4.5 times reduction in energy consumption in comparison to other prominent methods in this field. Furthermore, AppealNet offers a 2.5 times improvement in energy efficiency per top-1 accuracy, outperforming the current state-of-the-art approaches. The FAccT conference has been a leading platform for Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency research since 2018. This study conducts a comprehensive analysis of the conference's publications, examining the dominant research topics and evaluation methods used, as well as identifying areas where the research falls short and providing prospects for further advancement. The results reveal a diverse set of prominent research areas within the community, including accounting for biases, accountability through auditing, and the development of Fairness-Aware Machine Learning. Evaluation methods employed by the research community vary, encompassing both quantitative and qualitative approaches. However, upon closer inspection, several issues are identified, including a lack of diversity in the studied real-world applications, an overemphasis on algorithmic fairness, and insufficient consideration of the broader societal implications. Furthermore, the research is often limited to individual algorithms rather than comprehensive solutions; and, in many cases, the chosen evaluation methods may not be well-suited to address the research questions. This study also highlights the need for more diverse and representative problem domains, improved algorithmic solutions, and effective communication of the research findings to stakeholders. A mixed-methods approach is proposed to facilitate the development of effective solutions, including a quantitative analysis of the research publications and a qualitative survey of the views of FAccT conference chairs and authors. This study aims to provide a foundation for future research directions and serves as a guide for conducting research in the field. We introduce a new approach to evaluate reinforcement learning policies in a broad range of scenarios. Our method enables agents to automatically identify crucial states that, if mispredicted, can lead to significant performance degradation. These states are often scarce, yet critical for successful policy execution. By leveraging learned state predictions, our approach refines policies in a small, targeted subset of states, enhancing overall performance. Data visualizations are a primary method for presenting complex information in an engaging way, particularly across various fields such as climate science and geology. However, data visualizations often overlook the needs of experts who are visually impaired, hindering their access to crucial scientific data and information. This research explores the difficulties experienced by geoscience experts who are visually impaired in accessing data visualizations, a problem exacerbated by the lack of accessible data visualizations and communication barriers. We conducted a study involving 17 experts through semi-structured interviews and analyzed their experiences, difficulties, and strategies for accessing visual information. The study revealed four key areas of expertise required for visually impaired scientists to navigate data visualizations effectively: understanding the context, interpreting visual cues, using technology, and employing prior knowledge. This research contributes to the development of accessible data visualizations by identifying key barriers and providing recommendations for improving data visualization accessibility and communication. Furthermore, it highlights the importance of collaboration between experts and individuals with visual impairments in shaping data visualization design and communication. Ultimately, this research aims to promote inclusive data visualization design that is applicable across various fields, not just geoscience. Future work will involve developing guidelines for creating accessible data visualizations and improving information design to enhance the quality of life for individuals with visual impairments. This research also aims to serve as a foundation for future studies in this area.

A new global convergence metric for preconditioned iterative eigensolvers is introduced, leveraging a gradient descent approach. Ensuring the security of software through hardware support for memory protection is a fundamental requirement for processor design.  However, current x86-64 processors' memory protection mechanisms have significant limitations, which have led to the development of new instructions like SGX, SFENCE-VMA, and CLDEMOTE.  These instructions are intended to provide robust protection against malicious software, but their practical effectiveness is uncertain.  A comprehensive test suite is needed to evaluate the reliability of these new instructions, which should be cross-platform and adaptable to various processor architectures. Predicting traffic conditions is a key challenge in transportation systems, particularly in urban areas where traffic congestion often leads to frustrating traffic delays. Existing traffic forecasting methods primarily rely on real-time traffic data and historical patterns, but tend to overlook the dynamic nature of traffic flow. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach called the Dynamic Spatial-Temporal Focus Network (DST- Focus). By integrating real-time traffic dynamics and spatial relationships into a single model, DST-Focus can accurately identify and anticipate traffic disruptions before they occur, thereby minimizing their impact on traffic congestion. In our approach, we use a dynamic focus module to track changes in traffic patterns and a spatial focus module to capture the spatial relationships between different locations. By combining real-time traffic dynamics with spatial relationships, our model can effectively encode the dynamics of traffic flow. Furthermore, we employ a self-adaptive temporal module to adaptively learn temporal dependencies, and a temporal attention module to selectively focus on key temporal features. Our approach has been successfully tested on a large-scale real-world dataset, demonstrating its ability to predict traffic conditions more accurately than existing methods and providing valuable insights into traffic dynamics. Notably, DST-Focus can predict traffic incidents earlier than traditional methods, thereby enabling proactive measures to prevent congestion and reduce traffic delays. The source code for our approach is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengxueay/DST-Focus. We introduce Entailer, a large-scale model designed to generate concise and accurate natural language responses to given questions using relevant supporting information. Specifically, Entailer produces three key components: an answer, a justifications list, a justifications list order, and a source document identifier. This model is trained on a massive dataset of over 20 million passages containing over 300 million questions along with relevant answers and justifications. Entailer is an efficient, single-stream transformer model that processes queries and passages simultaneously, producing all required elements. Entailer is demonstrated to significantly outperform the existing benchmark in all requested aspects: providing justifications, creating coherent chains of reasoning, providing accurate answers, and accurately identifying sources. Notably, Entailer achieves this performance with a much faster processing time compared to the previous best model. Entailer is also shown to be adaptable, allowing it to successfully answer questions from new data sets, even those with different formats, when provided with relevant context. Additionally, Entailer is found to be effective in generating responses to questions that are similar to those in its training data. Entailer is available for public use, and its code is accessible at https://github.com/allenai/entailer. The corresponding data is available at https://huggingface.co/Entailer. The evaluation results are presented in the supplementary material. Entailer is further discussed in the paper "Entailing Answers with Context for Open and Adversarial Questions". This study introduces a cutting-edge deep learning model that employs audio input to diagnose respiratory failure in COVID-19 patients. The model leverages a combination of audio features extracted through Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients and spectrograms as well as Transformers to identify distinct patterns in patient breathing. The data collected comprises audio recordings from COVID-19 patients in intensive care units, including those on mechanical ventilation and those who weren't, spanning a total of 155 recordings. The proposed model achieves an impressive 94.37% accuracy in detecting ventilated COVID-19 patients, surpassing the performance of existing deep learning models and machine learning algorithms. Furthermore, the model's performance is enhanced when it is trained on data from mechanical ventilation patients only, resulting in 100% accuracy. The study also explores the model's interpretability using attention visualization, which sheds light on the distinctive audio patterns characteristic of ventilated COVID-19 patients. The study's findings have significant implications for developing an intelligent system to diagnose respiratory failure in COVID-19 patients. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to utilize Transformers for COVID-19 patient diagnosis. This research introduces an innovative tool for assessing conditional independence in graphical models called the regional permutation criterion. Through both theoretical and practical verification, we establish that this method effectively identifies all genuine conditional independence relationships within complex network structures. Furthermore, we have derived an exact formula to determine the expected number of permutation tests required for network validation and have confirmed that the regional permutation criterion not only outperforms existing methods under standard conditions but also exhibits robustness in the presence of non-linear effects and moderate deviations from normal distribution assumptions. Ultimately, we have demonstrated the practical application of these methods by analyzing a dataset related to Canadian urban indicators. Tags: Bayesian models, graphical models, conditional independence, permutation criteria, network analysis. Keywords: conditional independence, graphical models, permutation criterion, network analysis. An application of this research can be found in examining the conditional independence of various Canadian urban indicators. For example, we investigate whether the indicators 'per capita income' and 'average housing price' are conditionally independent when considered in conjunction with other variables such as population and language, and we find that they are not. Results of this study suggest that the regional permutation criterion is a powerful and reliable tool for identifying conditional independence relationships within complex network structures. A quantum field's expectation value, as expressed through field operators, may seem to imply a certain "locality of knowledge." However, upon closer examination, it's possible to argue that doing so necessitates localized measurement instruments, thus necessitating a revision of the traditional understanding of entanglement.

This concept is explored further through the study of free scalar fields in one spatial dimension, as well as a simplified, modified version of the Unruh-de Wittetsetup, where we derive explicit expressions for field operators in different regions of spacetime, demonstrating entanglement in a straightforward manner.

We also explore the application of this understanding to the Unruh-de Wittetsetup, as well as the free Dirac field scenario, as a means of illustrating the universality of our findings. Furthermore, we examine the possibility of entanglement detection through the study of correlations between field operators at the same location, as well as the possibility of using field operators to convey information about localized regions of spacetime. This is achieved by examining the vacuum excitation of a scalar field in a simplified, one-dimensional model. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the study of quantum fields in high-energy particle collisions. Arabic speakers face significant difficulties in typing using their native language, known as Arabizi, due to the absence of suitable input methods. This research aims to address this challenge by developing a system that predicts Arabizi input, taking into consideration the complexities of Arabic script. We propose a novel approach, based on the concept of Multi-Task Sequence Forecasting, to simultaneously predict multiple levels of Arabizi input, including character transliteration, diacritical marks, and standard Arabic. The proposed system is evaluated on a large-scale Tunisian dataset and achieves impressive results, surpassing existing state-of-the-art techniques by a significant margin. Furthermore, this study contributes a new, annotated Tunisian Arabizi dataset and a software tool, known as Arabizi-forecaster, to the research community. The proposed system is expected to be a valuable resource for Arabizi input and can potentially be adapted for other Arabizi dialects. The developed tool and dataset will be made publicly available. A novel approach to creating a multilevel coarse-grained model for machine learning is introduced, leveraging reinforcement learning to address complex complex physical systems. This innovative method begins by segmenting the system into individual components, represented by nodes, and employs a deep deterministic policy gradient algorithm to determine optimal nodes for coarse-graining. By integrating the learned coarse-grained model with a multigrid method, the proposed approach efficiently solves challenging nonlinear problems. Validation of the new approach is demonstrated through numerical simulations of the Stefan problem, a classic model describing melting in a multistage, nonlinear process. Results show that the developed coarse-grained model accurately captures the Stefan problem's behavior across various spatial and temporal resolutions, outperforming conventional approaches in terms of multigrid convergence rates. Furthermore, the proposed method's ability to create effective coarse-grained models enables the efficient resolution of the Stefan problem across diverse scales. Notably, this novel approach is highly adaptable and can be easily applied to a wide range of problems. Moreover, the developed algorithm is highly transferable, allowing for its successful application to other complex, nonlinear problems, such as the Brinkman equation and the Poisson equation with a random forcing term. Overall, this study presents a groundbreaking method for learning effective coarse-grained models, applicable to a broad spectrum of complex physical systems. This achievement is expected to have a profound impact on the development of machine learning techniques for modeling complex systems. In the field of data-driven decision-making, model evaluation is a crucial step. Assessing the uncertainty of a model's predictions is equally vital. However, when training data is limited, models may not capture the true uncertainty of their predictions. Transfer learning offers a solution, allowing models to leverage each other's knowledge. For transfer learning to be effective, it's essential to choose the optimal policy for each task. This paper explores the concept of optimal transfer learning through Bayesian methods. By analyzing the concept in the context of multiple tasks, we derived an analytical expression for evaluating the performance of these optimal policies. However, this expression is challenging to compute in practice. To address this issue, we developed a novel approach using importance sampling, which we then improved using a Monte Carlo method. This method, which we call RMCSF, was shown to be effective in small sample settings and was further enhanced to be resilient to overestimation. Through experiments on multiple tasks, we demonstrated the superiority of our approach over traditional methods. Our results also highlighted the importance of our approach in identifying overestimation problems, which other methods often struggle with. This research has significant implications for data-driven decision-making and is expected to have a broader impact on related fields. The presence of coronary artery calcium often serves as an indicator for potential coronary artery disease (CAD), enabling the prediction of future cardiovascular events. A novel method utilizing a convolutional neural network is proposed for identifying the type of Riemann surfaces within hyperelliptic curves. These representations are then used as input for a CNN to classify the Riemann surface. Trained models achieve high accuracy in categorizing genus 0 and 1 curves, with accuracy rates exceeding 99%. Additionally, the method is successfully applied to classify compact Riemann surfaces of genus 2. Notably, the method's ability to identify surfaces is validated through its correct classification of double covers of elliptic curves. Furthermore, the method is adapted to classify the topological types of plane curve arrangements, yielding a CNN that can accurately classify these arrangements up to degree 10. This method demonstrates the potential for identifying the topological type of curves solely based on the spectrum of their Gauss map. Although the method's accuracy is lower for curves of genus 2, further training on more extensive datasets is expected to significantly improve performance. Overall, the method's application of CNNs to spectral representations holds great promise for categorizing curves, with potential applications extending beyond Riemann surfaces. This study introduces a novel concept of non-log-concave sampling and develops a first-order stationary assurance framework for LMC in this context. We also propose a new type of gradient descent-ascent dynamics tailored for non-log-concave functions and demonstrate its convergence in this setting. Experimental results validate the theoretical findings, highlighting the framework's ability to provide first-order stationary assurances for non-log-concave targets. Furthermore, our results show that the proposed dynamic outperforms the traditional gradient descent-ascent dynamic with a single step size parameter in a wide range of cases. We also demonstrate that the new framework enhances the success probability of ensuring entropy increase in LMC sampling for non-log-concave targets. Additional experiments reveal that the proposed dynamic can accelerate convergence in certain cases, but may also decrease the convergence rate in other cases. Overall, our research provides a new understanding of the stationary behavior of LMC for non-log-concave functions and offers a more effective solution for such cases. The resulting data is then presented to the developers through a web-based interface that allows them to track how their call graphs have evolved over various versions of their software. The results from a pilot study indicate that developers can greatly benefit from this information when making decisions about their software systems, such as identifying areas that require refactoring or determining the feasibility of merging different versions of their code. The potential applications of this research are numerous, with possible extensions including the development of a tool that provides real-time call graph analytics or integration with other software analytics services to enhance their effectiveness. Time series data often exists in two or more related dimensions, such as electrical activity in the brain measured over time.  This paper explores the analysis of multivariate functional time series data that exhibits singularities, meaning the signal can be broken down into unique, disjoint components, each having a limited spatial or temporal scope. We introduce a method of singular spectrum analysis for one-dimensional time series and expand it to multi-dimensional time series to isolate these unique components, without requiring prior knowledge of the individual time series. Through simulated studies, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in separating distinct patterns of behavior and compare it to existing methods, highlighting its strengths and weaknesses. Furthermore, we apply this technique to a real-world dataset of brain activity measurements. This method is particularly useful for identifying complex patterns in high-dimensional data and distinguishing them from noise, without relying on prior knowledge. It can also be used to identify patterns in other types of data such as images and genetic sequences. The source code for this analysis is available on GitHub.

A novel direction of arrival (DOA) estimation method is proposed, which combines external microphone data with a neural network using GCC-PHAT features. The approach is designed to enhance the performance of embedded devices equipped with a microphone array, which often struggle due to limited spatial separation between speakers at close distances. To overcome this, we leverage a built-in microphone to extract features related to the speaker's location, which are then integrated with a neural network trained on array data. The results indicate that this hybrid method outperforms single-method approaches and traditional combinations, and achieves comparable results or better performance than existing multi-sensor fusion techniques. The approach is particularly effective in scenarios with low microphone separations, where it excels at estimating speaker locations. Additionally, we demonstrate the potential of this method in real-world applications by applying it to voice activity detection and speaker localization in a meeting recording. As video conferencing continues to evolve, the importance of efficient neural video compression grows due to the limitations of traditional methods in handling various content. The high computational demands of neural video codecs are a major obstacle, particularly in resource-constrained environments, where quality degradation often occurs when resources are insufficient. Current neural video compression solutions are vulnerable to errors caused by memory access misalignment, a problem exacerbated by the increasing use of specialized hardware. To address these challenges, we introduce Gemino, a novel neural video codec that offers a balance between quality and resource efficiency. By employing a memory layout that aligns with the natural order of video data, Gemino reduces errors caused by misalignment. We also propose a dynamic quality control mechanism that dynamically adjusts compression ratios based on available system resources. Furthermore, we introduce a memory resilience technique that minimizes errors resulting from misaligned memory access. Our results demonstrate that Gemino achieves a balance between quality and resilience, outperforming state-of-the-art solutions in both quality and resilience. A thorough analysis of Gemino's effectiveness across various scenarios, including mobile devices and cloud servers, highlights its potential for use in a wide range of applications. Ultimately, the design principles of Gemino can be applied to other neural video codecs, enabling a new generation of video codecs capable of handling a broad spectrum of content.

CMP's pre-training stage involves generating contrastive pairs of video and language segments, which are then used to learn representations that can capture both high-level semantic information and low-level visual and acoustic details. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to the development of several state-of-the-art salient object detection methods, yet most of these methods rely heavily on manually annotated saliency masks, which are time-consuming to obtain. To overcome this limitation, this study proposes a novel approach called Saliency Object Counting (SOC). By leveraging object counting techniques, SOC can simultaneously estimate both pixel-level and instance-level saliency maps without requiring explicit annotation. Specifically, SOC first generates a coarse pixel-level saliency map through a weakly-supervised network, and then uses this map to guide a fully-supervised instance detection network, resulting in refined saliency maps. Experimental results on five public salient object detection datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SOC in achieving comparable performance to top-tier fully-supervised methods. Moreover, SOC has shown a significant advantage in terms of speed, being up to 40 times faster than its fully-supervised counterparts.
